title: Reflections & Input Impedance
description: The complex reflection coefficient, return and mismatch loss, and the input impedance of terminated lines and stubs.

study.title: Complex loads, complex Γ
study.body: Communication Systems used Γ and VSWR for resistive loads. Real loads (antennas, transistor inputs) are complex, $Z_L = R_L + jX_L$, so $\Gamma_L$ is a complex number. Its **magnitude** says how much of the wave reflects, its **phase** θ where the standing-wave maxima and minima sit. Compute it as a complex division: divide the moduli of numerator $(R_L - Z_0) + jX_L$ and denominator $(R_L + Z_0) + jX_L$, and subtract their angles. θ has the sign of $X_L$: positive for inductive, negative for capacitive loads.

study.title: Explore: the standing wave of a complex load
study.body: At distance ℓ from the load the voltage is $|V(\ell)| = |V_0^+|\,|1 + \Gamma_L e^{-j2\beta\ell}|$. It swings between $1 + |\Gamma|$ and $1 - |\Gamma|$ and repeats every λ/2; the reflected wave travels the extra distance twice, hence the **2βℓ**. The phase θ shifts the pattern: the first maximum lies at $\theta\lambda/4\pi$ (for θ ≥ 0) and the first minimum at $(\theta + \pi)\lambda/4\pi$. Drag |Γ| and θ.

study.title: Return loss, mismatch loss, VSWR
study.body: Three ways to state one number, |Γ|. **Return loss** says how far the reflected wave is below the incident one (larger is better); **mismatch loss** how much less power the load gets than a matched load would. |Γ| is a voltage ratio, so use **20 log** for it and **10 log** for power ratios such as $1 - |\Gamma|^2$. Typical specs: RL = 10 dB means |Γ| = 0.32, VSWR 1.92, 10 % reflected and ML = 0.46 dB; RL = 20 dB means |Γ| = 0.1, VSWR 1.22, 1 % and 0.04 dB.

study.title: Input impedance of a terminated line
study.body: A lossless line of length ℓ transforms $Z_L$ into $Z_{in}$; only the electrical length βℓ = 2πℓ/λ matters. By hand, put $t = \tan\beta\ell$, split numerator $N$ and denominator $D$ into real and imaginary parts and divide: $N/D = N D^*/|D|^2$. Equivalently, rotate the reflection coefficient, $\Gamma_{in} = \Gamma_L e^{-j2\beta\ell}$, and convert back with $Z_{in} = Z_0(1+\Gamma_{in})/(1-\Gamma_{in})$.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& Z_{in} = Z_0\,\frac{Z_L + jZ_0\tan\beta\ell}{Z_0 + jZ_L\tan\beta\ell}\\ & N = R_L + j(X_L + Z_0t)\\ & D = (Z_0 - X_Lt) + jR_Lt\end{aligned}

study.title: λ/2 and λ/4 lines
study.body: At ℓ = λ/2, tan βℓ = 0 and the line repeats the load for any $Z_0$ (at that one frequency). At ℓ = λ/4 the tangent is infinite and the line **inverts** the impedance: a short becomes an open, a low resistance a high one, and a capacitive load looks inductive, because $1/(R + jX)$ flips the sign of the reactance. Example: a 50 Ω λ/4 line turns 25 − j25 Ω into 2500/(25 − j25) = 50 + j50 Ω.

study.title: Stubs as reactances
study.body: A shorted or open line has a purely imaginary input impedance, so at microwave frequencies a stub replaces an inductor or capacitor. Its reactance follows tan βℓ instead of ωL, so it changes faster with frequency and repeats every λ/2: a shorted stub that is λ/8 long at $f_0$ (X = +$Z_0$) is λ/4 long at $2f_0$, where it looks like an open circuit. The graph shows $X_{in}/Z_0$ of a shorted (blue) and an open (orange) stub.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& Z_{sc} = jZ_0\tan\beta\ell\\ & Z_{oc} = -jZ_0\cot\beta\ell\\ & L_{eq} = \frac{X}{\omega},\quad C_{eq} = \frac{-1}{\omega X}\end{aligned}

steps.title: Γ of a complex load
steps.body: For $Z_L = R_L + jX_L$ on a line $Z_0$, the reflection coefficient is a complex number. Numerator and denominator are $(R_L - Z_0) + jX_L$ and $(R_L + Z_0) + jX_L$: divide their magnitudes for $|\Gamma_L|$ and subtract their angles for θ. A passive load ($R_L \geq 0$) always gives $|\Gamma_L| \leq 1$.

steps.prompt: A {{Z0}} Ω line ends in a load with $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}} and $X_L$ = {{XL|Ω}}.

ask.prompt: Find $|\Gamma_L|$.
Find the phase θ of $\Gamma_L$ in degrees.
ask.explanation: Angle of the numerator $(R_L - Z_0) + jX_L$ = ({{RL-Z0}}) + j({{XL}}): {{a1}}°. Angle of the denominator {{RL+Z0}} + j({{XL}}): {{a2}}°. θ = {{a1}}° − ({{a2}}°) = **{{th}}°**. It has the sign of $X_L$: positive for an inductive, negative for a capacitive load.

steps.title: From |Γ| to VSWR, return loss and delivered power
steps.body: Only the magnitude counts for these: two loads with the same |Γ| but a different θ give the same VSWR and return loss. |Γ| is a ratio of voltages, so return loss uses 20 log; the power that reaches the load is a fraction $1 - |\Gamma|^2$ of the incident power, so mismatch loss uses 10 log.

steps.prompt: An antenna presents $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}, $X_L$ = {{XL|Ω}} to a 50 Ω feed line.

ask.prompt: Find the VSWR on the line.
ask.explanation: $|\Gamma|$ = √(({{RL-50}})² + ({{XL}})²) / √({{RL+50}}² + ({{XL}})²) = {{G}}. VSWR = (1 + {{G}})/(1 − {{G}}) = **{{(1+G)/(1-G)}}**. With a reactive load the VSWR is not simply $R_L/Z_0$.

ask.prompt: Find the return loss in dB.
What percentage of the incident power reaches the antenna?
ask.explanation: $|\Gamma|$ = {{G}}, so $|\Gamma|^2$ = {{100*G^2}} % is reflected and **{{100*(1-G^2)}} %** is delivered (mismatch loss {{-10*log10(1-G^2)}} dB).

steps.prompt: A network analyzer shows a return loss of {{RL}} dB for an antenna. What is the VSWR?
steps.explanation: |Γ| is a voltage ratio: $|\Gamma| = 10^{-RL/20}$ = {{G}}, and VSWR = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|) = **{{(1+G)/(1-G)}}**. Using $10^{-RL/10}$ = {{Gw}} would treat |Γ| as a power ratio and give {{(1+Gw)/(1-Gw)}}; 1 + |Γ| is only $V_{max}$ relative to the incident wave.

steps.prompt: Match each reflection coefficient magnitude to its return loss.
steps.explanation: RL = −20 log|Γ|: 0.1 → 20 dB, 0.316 = $10^{-0.5}$ → 10 dB, 0.5 → 6.02 dB, and a short or open (|Γ| = 1) → 0 dB: everything comes back.

steps.prompt: Two loads with the same $|\Gamma_L|$ but a different phase θ give the same VSWR and the same return loss.
steps.explanation: True. VSWR and return loss depend only on |Γ|. The phase θ only shifts the standing-wave pattern along the line: it decides where the maxima and minima lie.

steps.prompt: A transmitter sends {{P}} dBm of incident power down a lossless line into a load with VSWR {{S}}. How much power does the load absorb, in dBm?

lessons.title: Input impedance, λ/4 lines and stubs

steps.title: Input impedance
steps.body: A line of length ℓ between the load and the point where you look changes the impedance you see. Put $t = \tan(2\pi\ell/\lambda)$, write numerator $N = R_L + j(X_L + Z_0t)$ and denominator $D = (Z_0 - X_Lt) + jR_Lt$, and divide: $Z_{in} = Z_0 N D^*/|D|^2$.

steps.prompt: A {{RL|Ω}} resistor terminates a lossless 50 Ω line that is {{lf}} λ long.

ask.prompt: Find the real part of $Z_{in}$.
Find the imaginary part of $Z_{in}$ (with sign).

steps.title: λ/2 and λ/4
steps.body: A λ/2 line repeats the load: $Z_{in} = Z_L$. A λ/4 line inverts it: $Z_{in} = Z_0^2/Z_L$. The inversion also flips the sign of the reactance, so through a λ/4 line a capacitor looks like an inductor and a short looks like an open.

steps.prompt: A lossless 50 Ω line that is exactly λ/4 long ends in a capacitor with reactance $X_L$ = −{{X}} Ω. What does the input of the line look like?
steps.explanation: $Z_{in} = Z_0^2/Z_L$ = 2500/(−j{{X}}) = +j{{2500/X}} Ω: an **inductor**. Dividing by −j gives +j, so a λ/4 line turns a capacitive load into an inductive input. Only a short at the end would become an open.

steps.prompt: A λ/4 section of {{Z0}} Ω line is terminated in $R_L$ = {{R|Ω}}, $X_L$ = {{X|Ω}}.

ask.prompt: Find $R_{in}$.
Find $X_{in}$ (with sign).
ask.explanation: $Z_{in} = Z_0^2(R_L - jX_L)/(R_L^2 + X_L^2)$ with $R_L^2 + X_L^2$ = {{m2||5}}: $X_{in}$ = −{{Z0^2||4}} × ({{X}}) / {{m2||5}} = **{{-Z0^2*X/m2|Ω}}**. The sign flips: the λ/4 line swaps inductive and capacitive.

steps.title: Stubs replace L and C
steps.body: A shorted stub shorter than λ/4 is inductive; an open stub shorter than λ/4 is capacitive. To build a reactance $X$, solve the stub formula for βℓ. In microstrip, open stubs are popular because they need no via to ground.

steps.prompt: At {{f|Hz}} you want to replace a {{C|F}} capacitor to ground by an open-circuited 50 Ω stub. How long must the stub be, as a fraction of a wavelength (ℓ/λ)?
steps.explanation: The open stub gives $-jZ_0\cot\beta\ell$, which must equal $-j/(\omega C)$: $\tan\beta\ell = \omega C Z_0$ = 2π × {{f|Hz}} × {{C|F}} × 50 = {{k}}. βℓ = arctan({{k}}) = {{bl}} rad = {{deg(bl)}}°, so ℓ/λ = {{deg(bl)}}/360 = **{{bl/(2*pi)}}**.

steps.prompt: A shorted stub that is λ/8 long at 1 GHz looks like an open circuit at 2 GHz.
steps.explanation: True. The physical length is fixed, so at 2 GHz the stub is twice as many wavelengths long: λ/4. Then $jZ_0\tan 90°$ is infinite, an open circuit. At 1 GHz it was $jZ_0\tan 45° = +jZ_0$. Stubs are only equivalent to a given L or C near their design frequency.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the normalized input resistance $r_{in}$ (blue) and reactance $x_{in}$ (orange) of a lossless line ending in $z_L = r_L + jx_L$ with $r_L$ = {{rl}} and $x_L$ = {{xl}}, versus the line length. Drag ℓ to the length where $z_{in}$ is **purely real and larger than 1**.
steps.explanation: $z_{in}$ is real where $\Gamma_{in} = \Gamma_L e^{-j2\beta\ell}$ lies on the real axis. $\Gamma_L$ = {{G}}∠{{deg(th)}}°; it reaches angle 0 (a voltage **maximum**, $r_{in}$ = VSWR = {{(1+G)/(1-G)}}) after 2βℓ = θ, i.e. ℓ/λ = θ/720° = **{{lmax}}** (adding 0.5 if negative). λ/4 further on, $z_{in}$ is real again but smaller than 1: a voltage minimum.

steps.prompt: A 50 Ω line of length {{lf}} λ ends in $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}, $X_L$ = {{XL|Ω}}.

ask.prompt: Find $R_{in}$.
Find $X_{in}$ (with sign).

steps.prompt: At {{f|Hz}} a 50 Ω cable with velocity factor {{VF}} feeds a load with $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}, $X_L$ = {{XL|Ω}}. How far from the load is the first voltage **minimum**?
steps.explanation: $\Gamma_L = (Z_L - 50)/(Z_L + 50)$ = {{gr}} + j({{gi}}), so θ = {{deg(th)}}°. The first minimum sits where θ − 2βℓ = −180°: ℓ/λ = (θ + 180°)/720° = {{lm}}. On the cable λ = {{VF}} × 3 × $10^8$ / {{f|Hz}} = {{lam|m}}, so ℓ = **{{lm*lam|m}}**.

steps.prompt: Slotted-line measurement on a 50 Ω line: the VSWR is {{S}} and the first voltage minimum lies {{lm}} λ from the load.

ask.prompt: Find $R_L$.
Find $X_L$ (with sign).
ask.explanation: |Γ| = {{G}} and θ = 720° × {{lm}} − 180° = {{deg(th)}}°. $X_L = Z_0\cdot 2|\Gamma|\sin\theta/|1-\Gamma|^2$ with $|1-\Gamma|^2$ = {{q}}: $X_L$ = 50 × 2 × {{G}} × sin({{deg(th)}}°) / {{q}} = **{{100*G*sin(th)/q|Ω}}**. A first minimum within λ/4 of the load means a capacitive load, one between λ/4 and λ/2 an inductive load.

steps.prompt: A 50 Ω line ends in an **inductive** load $z_L$ = 0.6 + j0.8, so $\Gamma_L$ = 0.5∠+90°. Which graph shows |V| versus the distance ℓ from the load? (Each graph runs from the load, ℓ = 0, on the left to ℓ = λ/2 on the right.)
steps.explanation: $|V| \propto |1 + \Gamma_L e^{-j2\beta\ell}|$ peaks where θ − 2βℓ = 0: ℓ = θλ/4π = 90°/720° λ = **λ/8**, with the minimum λ/4 further on (at 3λ/8). An inductive load always puts a maximum first (within λ/4), a capacitive load a minimum first. A maximum right at the load means a resistance above $Z_0$, a minimum at the load one below $Z_0$.

steps.prompt: A shorted {{Z0}} Ω air line is {{len*1000}} mm long. At {{f|Hz}}:

ask.prompt: what is its input reactance?
ask.explanation: In air λ = c/f = {{3e8/f|m}}, so βℓ = 360° × {{len|m}} / {{3e8/f|m}} = {{deg(bl)}}°. $X_{in} = Z_0\tan\beta\ell$ = {{Z0}} × tan({{deg(bl)}}°) = **{{X|Ω}}** (inductive, since ℓ < λ/4).

ask.prompt: which inductance has the same reactance at this frequency?
ask.explanation: βℓ = {{deg(bl)}}°, so $X_{in}$ = {{Z0}} × tan({{deg(bl)}}°) = {{X|Ω}}. $L_{eq} = X/\omega$ = {{X}} / (2π × {{f|Hz}}) = **{{X/(2*pi*f)|H}}**. It only matches the stub near this frequency.

steps.prompt: Match the phase θ of $\Gamma_L$ to the kind of load.
steps.explanation: Im Γ has the sign of $X_L$, so the upper half (θ between 0° and 180°) holds inductive loads and the lower half capacitive ones. On the real axis the load is resistive: Γ > 0 for $R_L > Z_0$ (θ = 0°), Γ < 0 for $R_L < Z_0$ (θ = 180°).

steps.prompt: A matched generator ($Z_g = Z_0$) feeds a mismatched load through a lossless line. The power delivered to the load depends on the length of the line.
steps.explanation: False. The generator sees a different $Z_{in}$ for every length, but with $Z_g = Z_0$ the incident wave is always the same and nothing re-reflects at the generator. The load absorbs $P_{avs}(1 - |\Gamma_L|^2)$ for any length. Only with $Z_g \neq Z_0$ do re-reflections make the delivered power length-dependent.

steps.prompt: A matched signal source with an available power of {{P}} dBm drives a 50 Ω line ending in $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}, $X_L$ = {{XL|Ω}}. Find the mismatch loss in dB.
steps.explanation: $|\Gamma_L|$ = √(({{RL-50}})² + ({{XL}})²) / √({{RL+50}}² + ({{XL}})²) = {{G}}. ML = −10 log(1 − {{G^2}}) = **{{-10*log10(1-G^2)}} dB**, so the load receives {{P+10*log10(1-G^2)}} dBm instead of {{P}} dBm, whatever the line length.

steps.prompt: A λ/4 transformer of $Z_1$ = √(50 × {{RL}}) Ω matches a {{RL|Ω}} resistor to a 50 Ω line at $f_0$. The frequency is now {{k}} $f_0$.

ask.prompt: Find $|\Gamma_{in}|$ seen from the 50 Ω line.
Find the return loss in dB.
ask.explanation: At {{k}} $f_0$: βℓ = {{90*k}}°, $Z_{in}$ = {{Rin|Ω}} + j({{Xin|Ω}}) (with $Z_1$ = {{Z1|Ω}}), so $|\Gamma_{in}|$ = {{G}} and RL = −20 log({{G}}) = **{{-20*log10(G)}} dB**. At $f_0$ the return loss would be infinite.

steps.prompt: You measure the input of an unknown lossless cable with its far end shorted and then open: $Z_{sc}$ = j{{Xs|Ω}} and $Z_{oc}$ = −j{{abs(Xo)|Ω}}.

ask.prompt: Find its characteristic impedance.
ask.explanation: $Z_{sc}Z_{oc} = (jZ_0\tan\beta\ell)(-jZ_0\cot\beta\ell) = Z_0^2$, so $Z_0 = \sqrt{Z_{sc}Z_{oc}}$ = √({{Xs}} × {{abs(Xo)}}) = **{{Z0|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: Find its electrical length βℓ in degrees (between 0° and 90°).
ask.explanation: $Z_{sc}/Z_{oc} = -\tan^2\beta\ell$, so $\tan\beta\ell = \sqrt{X_{sc}/|X_{oc}|}$ = √({{Xs}}/{{abs(Xo)}}) = {{tan(rad(bl))}} and βℓ = **{{bl}}°**. (Check: $Z_0$ = √({{Xs}} × {{abs(Xo)}}) = {{Z0}} Ω and {{Z0}} × tan {{bl}}° = {{Xs}} Ω.)

steps.prompt: A capacitor with reactance −{{Xc}} Ω terminates a lossless 50 Ω line that is {{lf}} λ long. The input impedance is purely reactive. Find $X_{in}$ (with sign).
steps.explanation: With $Z_L = jX_L$ the formula stays imaginary: $Z_{in} = jZ_0\frac{X_L + Z_0t}{Z_0 - X_Lt}$. $t$ = tan({{360*lf}}°) = {{t}}, so $X_{in}$ = 50 × (−{{Xc}} + 50 × {{t}}) / (50 + {{Xc}} × {{t}}) = **{{Xin|Ω}}**. A lossless line with a reactive load is just another reactance, like a stub.

steps.prompt: A shorted cable stub is {{len*1000}} mm long and has a velocity factor of {{VF}}.

ask.prompt: At what lowest frequency does its input look like an open circuit?
ask.explanation: A shorted stub looks open when it is λ/4 long: $\lambda$ = 4 × {{len*1000}} mm, so $f = v_p/\lambda$ = {{VF}} × 3 × $10^8$ / (4 × {{len|m}}) = **{{VF*3e8/(4*len)|Hz}}**.

ask.prompt: At what lowest frequency is its input reactance $+Z_0$?

steps.prompt: An incident wave of {{Vp|V}} amplitude travels on a 50 Ω line toward a load with $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}, $X_L$ = {{XL|Ω}}.

ask.prompt: What is the largest voltage amplitude anywhere on the line?
ask.explanation: $|\Gamma_L|$ = √(({{RL-50}})² + ({{XL}})²) / √({{RL+50}}² + ({{XL}})²) = {{G}}. Where incident and reflected waves are in phase: $V_{max} = |V_0^+|(1 + |\Gamma|)$ = {{Vp}} × {{1+G}} = **{{Vp*(1+G)|V}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the smallest voltage amplitude on the line?
ask.explanation: $|\Gamma_L|$ = {{G}}. Where the waves are in antiphase: $V_{min} = |V_0^+|(1 - |\Gamma|)$ = {{Vp}} × {{1-G}} = **{{Vp*(1-G)|V}}**. Ratio: VSWR = {{(1+G)/(1-G)}}.

steps.prompt: Put the steps in order to compute $Z_{in}$ of a terminated line by hand.
items: Find the electrical length βℓ = 360° · ℓ/λ
Form $N = R_L + j(X_L + Z_0t)$ and $D = (Z_0 - X_Lt) + jR_Lt$
steps.explanation: Everything depends on the electrical length, so start there. Then the tangent, then numerator and denominator as real and imaginary parts, a complex division (multiply by the conjugate of D) and finally scale by $Z_0$. Cross-check by rotating Γ by −2βℓ.

steps.prompt: A shorted stub that replaces a 2 nH inductor at 2 GHz also behaves like a 2 nH inductor at 4 GHz.
steps.explanation: False. A stub's reactance is $Z_0\tan\beta\ell$, and βℓ doubles when the frequency doubles. A lumped inductor's reactance grows linearly with f, but tan grows faster and becomes infinite at λ/4, so the 'equivalent inductance' $X/\omega$ changes with frequency. Stubs mimic L and C only near the design frequency.
